subject: Archaeology
title: Digital Preservation of Mesopotamia
description: Learn Digital Preservation of Mesopotamia in one minute.

hook.text: You cannot bomb a 3D scan. Digital archives are now the last line of defense for Mesopotamia's threatened heritage.

buildup.text: Before ISIS advanced, teams raced to 3D-scan Palmyra, Nimrud, and Hatra.

discovery.text: The CDLI project has digitized over 350,000 cuneiform tablets.

twist.text: A replica of Palmyra's Arch of Triumph was 3D-printed and displayed in Trafalgar Square — a digital ghost of the original.

climax.text: AI is now reading broken and eroded tablets faster than humans.

punchline.text: The originals can be bombed. The scans live forever.

quiz.question: What is the CDLI project?
options: A crowdfunding platform to restore damaged Mesopotamian sites
A digital archive of over 350,000 cuneiform tablets accessible online
A training program for Iraqi archaeologists working in conflict zones

details.summary: Digital technologies including 3D scanning, satellite imagery, and AI-powered cuneiform reading are transforming Mesopotamian archaeology. Threatened and destroyed sites are being digitally reconstructed, and millions of unread tablets are becoming accessible through machine learning.
details.whyItMatters: Digital preservation ensures that even physically destroyed heritage survives in virtual form. AI translation of cuneiform tablets promises to unlock knowledge from hundreds of thousands of unread documents within our lifetimes.
takeaways: 3D scanning preserves threatened and destroyed sites digitally
AI is accelerating the translation of unread cuneiform tablets
Satellite imagery monitors site damage and looting in real time

faq.question: Can AI really read cuneiform tablets?
faq.answer: Increasingly, yes. Machine learning models trained on already-translated tablets can now suggest readings for damaged or unclear signs. They cannot replace expert scholars yet, but they dramatically accelerate the process of making the vast cuneiform corpus accessible.

faq.question: How does satellite imagery help Mesopotamian archaeology?
faq.answer: Satellites detect looting pits, track site destruction during conflict, and identify buried structures through vegetation and soil patterns. Corona spy satellite images from the 1960s have revealed ancient sites now covered by modern development or damaged by recent conflicts.
